headline: High risk of prompt-injection, data leakage, and cascading errors from shared MCP/stdin-stdout workflows with broad egress and mutable state.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents expose MCP and stdin/stdout surfaces, so content can cross between them through shared orchestration or copy-paste. agent_a also uses hooks/workers and agent_b can observe/replace/block lifecycle payloads, making instruction smuggling plausible. No direct shared channel is documented, so I do not escalate to high.
conditions: IF the two agents are connected by a shared MCP server or stdio bridge, injection risk becomes active.
IF agent_b consumes agent_a output as instructions without provenance checks, injected text can steer tool use.
mitigations: Disable automatic instruction-following on imported text.
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent messages.
Require a human review step before executing tool calls from the other agent.
Restrict shared MCP endpoints to read-only where possible.
requires-engineering: implement content-sanitization and provenance enforcement in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches code, repository metadata, task prompts, and Ed25519 signatures; agent_b touches conversations, long-term memory, tool results, and workflow state. Both have network egress and MCP, so sensitive context can flow outward if they share a workspace or relay. The pairwise leakage path is plausible but not directly evidenced, so medium fits.
conditions: IF the agents share a filesystem, prompts or signatures from agent_a can be exposed to agent_b.
IF agent_b forwards tool results or memory to its backend, data from agent_a can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and credentials per agent.
Turn off shared clipboard or shared mounts.
Redact secrets before passing outputs between agents.
Limit outbound destinations to allowlisted hosts only.
requires-engineering: add per-field data-loss prevention and egress auditing.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can spawn subprocesses, use MCP, and support multiple instances; agent_a can execute shell, install packages, and modify git state, while agent_b has broad network egress and browser execution. If they operate on the same repo or mutable workspace, concurrent writes and git mutations can race and corrupt state. The overlap is dangerous by default once co-located.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same repository or directory, file and git conflicts can occur.
IF both are launched concurrently without locking, one agent can overwrite the other's artifacts.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Serialize git writes with a lock.
Disable package installation in one agent during shared runs.
Use per-agent branches or sandboxes.
requires-engineering: add workspace-level concurrency control and conflict detection.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a produces analysis and can modify git state; agent_b handles tool results, workflow state, and provenance metadata, so it can easily treat upstream output as authoritative. With both agents supporting MCP and subprocesses, a bad assumption from agent_a can cascade into agent_b actions or persisted state. No verification step is documented, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output without validation, errors can propagate into workflow state.
IF agent_a's generated artifacts are committed or reused, downstream actions can amplify mistakes.
mitigations: Insert a validation step between agents.
Require schema checks on all handoff payloads.
Mark agent_a outputs as untrusted by default.
Review any commit or action generated from agent outputs.
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks before downstream execution.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and do not declare regulated-data certifications, residency constraints, or retention policies. The only concrete compliance concern is that agent_a handles task prompts and signatures while agent_b handles conversations and memory, but no specific residency mismatch is documented. I therefore keep this low rather than infer a breach.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is routed through either agent, compliance review becomes necessary.
IF deployment policy requires certified processing or fixed residency, the missing declarations become a gap.
mitigations: Confirm data-class handling before deployment.
Avoid sending regulated data to either agent.
Document retention and deletion behavior.
Pin deployment region and hosting provider.
requires-engineering: obtain formal compliance attestations or DPA coverage.
